title: Global Institutions, Rights, Citizenship, Sustainability & Food Security
subject: The Contemporary World
description: State vs. nation vs. colony, UN 6 main organs, WTO/IMF/World Bank, UDHR & ICJ vs. ICC, asylum & refugees, global citizenship roles, UNSC veto, Paris Agreement, and the 4 pillars of food security.

questions.question: In Reading Material 1, when imported fuel prices rise and businesses raise food delivery prices as a result, what concept does this illustrate?
options: Interdependence among countries
Complete local self-isolation
Colony status
Regional veto power
questions.answer: Interdependence among countries
questions.explanation: Interdependence means distant economic or environmental events directly affect daily prices, jobs, and supplies locally.

questions.question: How does a Filipino working abroad sending money home illustrate the multiple dimensions of globalization?
options: It connects economies via financial remittances while exchanging customs and cultures across borders
It proves globalization affects only politicians
It stops cross-border communication
It prevents cultural exchange
questions.answer: It connects economies via financial remittances while exchanging customs and cultures across borders
questions.explanation: Remittances support education and food at home while workers both share Filipino customs and learn host cultures.

questions.question: Why do some individuals benefit more from global connections than others according to Reading Material 1?
options: Because access to reliable internet, money, and educational/economic opportunities is unevenly distributed
Because only large countries can be states
Because interdependence guarantees equal wealth for everyone
Because fuel prices never change
questions.answer: Because access to reliable internet, money, and educational/economic opportunities is unevenly distributed
questions.explanation: Global connections widen opportunities yet reproduce disparities when access to resources is unequal.

questions.question: How do a 'state,' a 'nation,' and a 'colony' differ in world affairs?
options: A state has people, territory, government, and independent external relations; a nation is a group sharing identity/history/belonging; a colony is controlled by another country and lacks full independence.
A state must always be giant in size; a nation is a treaty; a colony has full sovereignty.
State and nation are 100% identical.
A colony has veto power in the UN Security Council.
questions.answer: A state has people, territory, government, and independent external relations; a nation is a group sharing identity/history/belonging; a colony is controlled by another country and lacks full independence.
questions.explanation: A single state can encompass diverse communities and national identities, regardless of geographic size.

questions.question: What is 'sovereignty,' and what is 'regionalism' (exemplified by ASEAN)?
options: Sovereignty: a state's authority over domestic affairs and independence abroad; Regionalism: cooperation among neighboring countries within a region on shared concerns.
Sovereignty: total world government; Regionalism: banning trade with neighbors.
Sovereignty: joining the ICC; Regionalism: vetoing treaties.
Sovereignty: UN Secretariat staff; Regionalism: IMF loans.
questions.answer: Sovereignty: a state's authority over domestic affairs and independence abroad; Regionalism: cooperation among neighboring countries within a region on shared concerns.
questions.explanation: Even when joining international agreements, national governments remain essential for services, rights protection, and domestic implementation.

questions.question: Which of the United Nations' six main organs holds the primary responsibility for international peace and security, and which organ has suspended regular operations after overseeing territories toward self-government?
options: Security Council (peace & security); Trusteeship Council (suspended regular operations)
General Assembly (peace & security); Secretariat (suspended)
ECOSOC (peace & security); ICJ (suspended)
ICC (peace & security); WTO (suspended)
questions.answer: Security Council (peace & security); Trusteeship Council (suspended regular operations)
questions.explanation: The 6 UN organs are General Assembly, Security Council, ECOSOC, Secretariat, International Court of Justice (ICJ), and Trusteeship Council.

questions.question: Match the General Assembly, ECOSOC, and Secretariat to their UN responsibilities:
options: General Assembly: universal discussion forum; ECOSOC: coordinates development & social work; Secretariat: handles daily administrative work
General Assembly: prosecutes individuals; ECOSOC: lends bailout funds; Secretariat: vetoes resolutions
General Assembly: handles daily work; ECOSOC: resolves border wars; Secretariat: debates treaties
All three have identical judicial powers
questions.answer: General Assembly: universal discussion forum; ECOSOC: coordinates development & social work; Secretariat: handles daily administrative work
questions.explanation: Each of the UN's six main bodies plays a distinct institutional role.

questions.topic: WTO vs. IMF vs. World Bank
questions.question: How do the core mandates of the WTO, IMF, and World Bank differ?
options: WTO: trade rules, agreements & trade disputes; IMF: financial/economic stability & conditional balance-of-payment loans; World Bank: long-term development, infrastructure & poverty reduction
WTO: criminal trials; IMF: climate treaties; World Bank: peacekeeping troops
WTO: poverty loans; IMF: tariffs; World Bank: daily UN admin
All three exist solely to print US dollars
questions.answer: WTO: trade rules, agreements & trade disputes; IMF: financial/economic stability & conditional balance-of-payment loans; World Bank: long-term development, infrastructure & poverty reduction
questions.explanation: Although their work can overlap, the WTO, IMF, and World Bank serve distinct functions in the global economy.

questions.question: What is the key legal difference between an international 'treaty' and a 'declaration' (such as the UDHR)?
options: A treaty creates binding legal duties for joining countries, whereas a declaration sets out shared principles or standards (though its principles often shape later treaties and laws)
A declaration automatically imposes military sanctions; a treaty is informal
Treaties are signed only by NGOs; declarations are signed only by businesses
There is no difference between them
questions.answer: A treaty creates binding legal duties for joining countries, whereas a declaration sets out shared principles or standards (though its principles often shape later treaties and laws)
questions.explanation: The UDHR (1948) is a foundational declaration rather than a treaty, yet deeply influences international and domestic law.

questions.question: Why does Reading Material 4 state that 'fair access to resources' is integral to human rights?
options: Because rights matter in daily life—children need schooling, and communities need safe water and protection from violence, especially when facing greater barriers
Because human dignity depends on a person's income or nationality
Because only citizens of rich nations have rights
Because declarations eliminate all barriers instantly without effort
questions.answer: Because rights matter in daily life—children need schooling, and communities need safe water and protection from violence, especially when facing greater barriers
questions.explanation: People never lose inherent dignity because of nationality, income, religion, or background.

questions.question: How do the International Court of Justice (ICJ) and the International Criminal Court (ICC) differ?
options: ICJ is a main UN organ handling legal disputes between states; ICC is a separate court (not a main UN organ) prosecuting individuals accused of very serious international crimes
ICJ prosecutes individual criminals; ICC settles trade tariffs
Both are identical chambers inside the WTO
ICC replaces every local police station and court in all countries
questions.answer: ICJ is a main UN organ handling legal disputes between states; ICC is a separate court (not a main UN organ) prosecuting individuals accused of very serious international crimes
questions.explanation: The ICC complements—rather than replaces—national courts, and an accusation alone never proves guilt.

questions.question: Which statement accurately describes international refugee and asylum protection in Reading Material 4?
options: Entering without usual documents automatically disqualifies an asylum claim, and countries can return refugees to any danger immediately

Asylum claims must be assessed fairly even without usual entry documents, and refugee protection includes a rule against returning people to certain serious dangers (non-refoulement)—though it does not grant an unlimited right to settle anywhere
People moving purely for jobs or study receive automatic refugee status
Host communities require no support when receiving refugees
questions.answer: Asylum claims must be assessed fairly even without usual entry documents, and refugee protection includes a rule against returning people to certain serious dangers (non-refoulement)—though it does not grant an unlimited right to settle anywhere
questions.explanation: Refugee protection balances fair assessment and safety from persecution with fair procedures and support for host communities.

questions.question: What does 'global citizenship' mean—and what does it NOT mean—according to Reading Material 5?
options: It means recognizing our connection and responsibility to people beyond our borders; it does NOT replace national citizenship or grant a 'world passport'
It means renouncing your home country's passport
It means ignoring local community problems
It means forcing every culture to adopt identical food and dress
questions.answer: It means recognizing our connection and responsibility to people beyond our borders; it does NOT replace national citizenship or grant a 'world passport'
questions.explanation: Caring about one's own community and respecting people elsewhere go hand in hand.

questions.question: How are 'global competence,' 'social responsibility,' and 'global civic engagement' defined?
options: Global competence: understanding wider issues & communicating across differences; Social responsibility: considering how actions affect others; Global civic engagement: participating in public concerns with wider awareness
Global competence: memorizing flags; Social responsibility: avoiding public life; Civic engagement: online gaming
All three mean maximizing personal profit at others' expense
They apply only to diplomats over age 50
questions.answer: Global competence: understanding wider issues & communicating across differences; Social responsibility: considering how actions affect others; Global civic engagement: participating in public concerns with wider awareness
questions.explanation: Listening, verifying facts, supporting education, and peaceful conflict resolution put these values into action.

questions.question: Does respecting other cultures require accepting harmful practices according to Reading Material 5?
options: Yes—cultural respect forbids questioning any practice
No—respecting culture means understanding without stereotyping, yet we can still raise concerns about harm while listening and treating communities with dignity
Only if a treaty allows it
Respecting culture means avoiding all contact with other societies
questions.answer: No—respecting culture means understanding without stereotyping, yet we can still raise concerns about harm while listening and treating communities with dignity
questions.explanation: Dignity and dialogue allow addressing harm without stereotyping entire communities.

questions.question: Match each global role from Reading Material 6: Global Reformer, Transnational Activist, and Politically Conscious Regionalist.
options: Global reformer: improves unfair policies (e.g., labor/education); Transnational activist: collaborates across borders on shared campaigns; Regionalist: supports regional cooperation (e.g., ASEAN)
Global reformer: blocks UN votes; Transnational activist: avoids foreign groups; Regionalist: closes regional borders
All three refer exclusively to corporate CEOs
None of these roles can overlap
questions.answer: Global reformer: improves unfair policies (e.g., labor/education); Transnational activist: collaborates across borders on shared campaigns; Regionalist: supports regional cooperation (e.g., ASEAN)
questions.explanation: Roles such as businessperson, environmental manager, reformer, activist, and regionalist frequently overlap.

questions.question: In Reading Material 6, what responsibility accompanies an 'elite global businessperson' and a 'global environmental manager'?
options: Only maximizing quarterly stock prices
Business influence brings responsibility toward workers, communities, and the environment; environmental managers track pollution/supply chains and ensure 'eco-friendly' claims are backed by evidence
Printing green logos without checking suppliers
Avoiding international networks
questions.answer: Business influence brings responsibility toward workers, communities, and the environment; environmental managers track pollution/supply chains and ensure 'eco-friendly' claims are backed by evidence
questions.explanation: Evidence-based environmental stewardship prevents misleading greenwashing.

questions.question: Why can shared UN action sometimes be blocked even when a clear majority of countries support it?
options: Because the five permanent members of the UN Security Council can use their veto power to block substantive decisions
Because the General Assembly never meets
Because the Trusteeship Council vetoes all budgets
Because ASEAN controls UN voting
questions.answer: Because the five permanent members of the UN Security Council can use their veto power to block substantive decisions
questions.explanation: Unequal power, lack of funding/staff, and conflicting national policies make global cooperation challenging.

questions.question: How is 'sustainability' defined, and what important detail does Reading Material 7 note about the 2015 Paris Agreement?
options: Sustainability meets present needs while protecting future generations' conditions; the Paris Agreement is a legally binding 2015 climate treaty where countries share plans, though it lacks automatic punishments for missed targets
Sustainability prioritizes jobs regardless of water or health damage; Paris Agreement imposes automatic prison sentences
Paris Agreement is a 1948 non-binding trade memo
Sustainability ignores future generations
questions.answer: Sustainability meets present needs while protecting future generations' conditions; the Paris Agreement is a legally binding 2015 climate treaty where countries share plans, though it lacks automatic punishments for missed targets
questions.explanation: True sustainability links human well-being with environmental care across generations.

questions.question: What are the four FAO pillars that explain 'food security' in Reading Material 7?
options: Availability, Access, Utilization, and Stability
Production, Tariffs, Exports, and Surplus
Farming, Packaging, Advertising, and Disposal
Calories, Sugar, Salt, and Oil
questions.answer: Availability, Access, Utilization, and Stability
questions.explanation: Food security requires food to be present (availability), obtainable/affordable (access), nutritious/safe (utilization), and reliable over time (stability).

questions.question: A local market has plenty of rice, fish, and vegetables, yet a family cannot afford balanced meals—and after a typhoon, washed-out roads halt food deliveries. Which food security pillars are failing?
options: Access (affordability and physical delivery) and Stability (continuity over time), even when food is available in the region
Availability only
Global citizenship
Trusteeship
questions.answer: Access (affordability and physical delivery) and Stability (continuity over time), even when food is available in the region
questions.explanation: Having food physically produced somewhere does not guarantee households can afford or reliably reach it.

questions.question: Within the four pillars of food security, what does 'Utilization' specifically concern?
options: Nutrition, food safety, clean preparation, and the bodily/sanitary conditions needed to benefit from food
Exporting crops to wealthier nations
Building highway tollbooths
Printing grocery receipts
questions.answer: Nutrition, food safety, clean preparation, and the bodily/sanitary conditions needed to benefit from food
questions.explanation: Utilization ensures food actually nourishes people safely rather than causing illness or malnutrition.

questions.question: According to Reading Material 7 ('Choices for the coming years'), why is inventing a useful new agricultural or energy technology not enough by itself?
options: Because communities also need money, skills, and supporting infrastructure (storage, transport, etc.) to actually access and use it
Because technology always makes farming worse
Because 2050 is already completely predetermined
Because waste has zero effect on food supply
questions.answer: Because communities also need money, skills, and supporting infrastructure (storage, transport, etc.) to actually access and use it
questions.explanation: Multi-level action across individuals, businesses, governments, and IGOs shapes a sustainable 2050.

questions.question: When world leaders hold summits and issue promises to act on global crises, what does Reading Material 3 remind us is still needed for real impact?
options: Funding, clear responsibilities, and concrete implementation/follow-through
Simply repeating the speech online
Waiting for another summit ten years later
Suspending all national governments
questions.answer: Funding, clear responsibilities, and concrete implementation/follow-through
questions.explanation: International organizations rely on member state resources and genuine execution to turn pledges into results.

questions.question: What misconception about the International Criminal Court (ICC) does Reading Material 4 clarify regarding national authority?
options: Claims about national authority do not automatically settle whether an international court can hear a case—its specific legal authority/jurisdiction must be examined
Any tweet automatically convicts a suspect at the ICC
The ICC is part of the UN Trusteeship Council
The ICC handles only commercial trademark lawsuits
questions.answer: Claims about national authority do not automatically settle whether an international court can hear a case—its specific legal authority/jurisdiction must be examined
questions.explanation: International criminal jurisdiction depends on legal treaties, complementarity, and factual evidence.

questions.question: Facing thorny challenges like sharing refugee costs, fair vaccine/medical supply distribution, and cyberattack responses, what three practices improve international cooperation?
options: Clear responsibilities, honest reporting, and participation from affected communities
Hidden budgets, unilateral vetoes, and excluding local communities
Cutting off all international flights
Replacing treaties with rumors
questions.answer: Clear responsibilities, honest reporting, and participation from affected communities
questions.explanation: Transparency and inclusion help bridge uneven power and resource gaps.

questions.question: When the International Monetary Fund (IMF) lends money to member states experiencing severe balance-of-payment crises, what often accompanies its assistance?
options: Policy conditions aimed at restoring financial and macroeconomic stability
Automatic UN Security Council permanent seats
Free military equipment
Zero accountability or reporting
questions.answer: Policy conditions aimed at restoring financial and macroeconomic stability
questions.explanation: IMF conditionality is a frequent topic of debate regarding national policy autonomy vs. economic stabilization.

questions.question: Which global institution specifically focuses on long-term development, reducing poverty, and financing infrastructure and public services?
options: The World Bank
The International Criminal Court
The Trusteeship Council
UNESCO alone
questions.answer: The World Bank
questions.explanation: While the IMF focuses on short/medium-term monetary stability and WTO on trade rules, the World Bank targets long-term poverty reduction and development.

questions.question: In Reading Material 5 ('Turning concern into action'), what principle balances claiming rights?
options: Rights come with responsibilities toward others—wanting a clean environment requires helping protect it, and valuing peace requires supporting dialogue
Rights mean taking whatever you want without considering neighbors
Responsibilities apply only to foreign governments
Helping communities means ignoring what they actually need
questions.answer: Rights come with responsibilities toward others—wanting a clean environment requires helping protect it, and valuing peace requires supporting dialogue
questions.explanation: Effective aid and solidarity respond to people's real needs and respect their agency.

questions.question: Which practical everyday actions does Reading Material 7 highlight as connecting individuals to global sustainability and food security?
options: Checking information, avoiding food/resource waste, respecting others, and joining credible community efforts
Hoarding excess plastic packaging
Ignoring damaged local infrastructure
Sharing unverified rumors
questions.answer: Checking information, avoiding food/resource waste, respecting others, and joining credible community efforts
questions.explanation: Individual habits reinforce national and international action across levels.

questions.question: How does ASEAN illustrate 'regionalism' in Southeast Asia?
options: Neighboring Southeast Asian countries collaborate on shared concerns like regional trade, migration, and natural resources
It acts as a single world government over Europe and Africa
It bans member states from speaking to each other
It replaces all national constitutions
questions.answer: Neighboring Southeast Asian countries collaborate on shared concerns like regional trade, migration, and natural resources
questions.explanation: Regionalism addresses cross-border challenges at a neighborhood scale.

questions.question: Besides increasing harvests, what practical measures listed in Reading Material 7 strengthen long-term food security?
options: Better food storage, stronger transport systems, healthy soil, support for farmers, and reducing food waste
Destroying rural roads
Exporting all water supplies
Closing local markets
questions.answer: Better food storage, stronger transport systems, healthy soil, support for farmers, and reducing food waste
questions.explanation: Post-harvest storage and resilient transport directly protect availability, access, and stability.

questions.question: What does Reading Material 1 mean by 'a local problem may have causes beyond the community, and a local action may affect people elsewhere'?
options: Local prices, jobs, weather, and consumption choices are embedded in global economic, cultural, and environmental networks
Local communities have zero connection to the outside world
Only big capital cities experience globalization
Global problems never affect rural areas
questions.answer: Local prices, jobs, weather, and consumption choices are embedded in global economic, cultural, and environmental networks
questions.explanation: Understanding the contemporary world begins with noticing how everyday life links local and global realities.

questions.question: Why does Reading Material 4 distinguish between people moving primarily for jobs or study and refugees seeking asylum?
options: Refugees cross borders fleeing persecution or serious danger and invoke specific protection rules against forced return to harm, unlike voluntary labor/study migrants
Students are never allowed to study abroad
Refugees travel only for tourism
Countries have no fair procedures for either group
questions.answer: Refugees cross borders fleeing persecution or serious danger and invoke specific protection rules against forced return to harm, unlike voluntary labor/study migrants
questions.explanation: International refugee law specifically protects people facing persecution or grave danger.

questions.question: Which official sources are cited in Reading Material 8 for food security and climate treaty concepts?
options: Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) for food security concepts, and UNFCCC for the Paris Agreement (alongside UN, WTO, IMF, ICC, and UNHCR)
NASA and FIFA
Hollywood Studios and Wall Street
OPEC and NATO
questions.answer: Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) for food security concepts, and UNFCCC for the Paris Agreement (alongside UN, WTO, IMF, ICC, and UNHCR)
questions.explanation: Knowing the official specialized institutions helps verify global data and policy claims.
